summary: An interpretable neural network, SPACER, learns the rules of cellular recruitment directly from tissue spatial transcriptomics data. Analyses of multiple cancers reveal a role for the local antigen presentation machinery and tumour mucins in T cell recruitment to tumours, and a mouse model of severe checkpoint inhibitor-induced myocarditis identifies CD4+ T cells as key disease effectors.
title: An interpretable AI model decodes the rules of cell recruitment to specific destinations
Engineering gut microbiome states overcomes hepatic accumulation of nanomedicines

summary: Advances in organoids, organs-on-chips and microphysiological systems are bringing human tissue models closer to the physiological complexity needed to study disease, evaluate therapies and inform precision medicine.
title: Towards physiologically relevant human tissue models

summary: Judicious animal model design and selection, rather than experimental excess, is key to generating robust, informative and ethically responsible evidence in biomedical research.
title: Animal numbers are not a proxy for scientific strength

summary: Six years and more than 250 lectures after its launch as a pandemic response, Tissue Talks has reached over 50,000 attendees across more than 80 countries, offering a blueprint for how biomedical communities can maintain continuous global connection beyond the annual conference cycle.
title: From pandemic response to a global scientific network via Tissue Talks

summary: Single-cell resolution spatial transcriptomics provides a great opportunity to explore the complex cellular contents in different tissues. Here we introduce SpatialZoomer, a spectral graph-based method that applies a set of low-pass filters to efficiently extract spatial molecular features from spatial transcriptomics data at multiple resolutions or scales, including the single cell scale, the niche scale with dozens of closely interacting cells and the domain scale with spatially organized cell contents. The corresponding critical scales can be automatically identified by partitioning a cross-scale similarity map. Results show that SpatialZoomer can identify disease-progression signals at specific scales in Alzheimer's disease and spatial context-dependent cell subtypes in tumour microenvironment. The extracted multi-scale features also uncovered spatially heterogeneous niches in cancer. SpatialZoomer achieves comparable or superior performance to existing methods for single-scale tasks, and it also has the advantages of high computational efficiency and low hardware requirements.
title: SpatialZoomer: multi-scale feature analysis of spatial transcriptomics

summary: Despite growing clinical adoption of artificial intelligence in radiology, fewer than one in five commercially available models are cleared for paediatric use. Existing systems are trained predominantly on adult data and generalize poorly to neonates, yet efficient strategies for repurposing them without data sharing or large-scale local data curation are lacking. Here we present an international retrospective study of neonatal chest radiographs from 30 neonatal intensive care units across 20 countries and territories, evaluating continual learning as a privacy-preserving approach to adapt a deep learning model for adult endotracheal tube assessment to neonatal care. Each hospital contributed 50 radiographs for sequential model retraining without centralized data pooling. Continual learning achieved lower anatomical landmark localization error (0.67 cm versus 1.29 cm for hospital-specific fine-tuning and 4.30 cm for adult-only models) at 29 of 30 sites, with improved detection of deep intubations at 27 of 30 sites. These findings demonstrate that privacy-preserving collaborative learning can address critical gaps in paediatric AI deployment.
title: Repurposing adult AI radiograph models for neonatal care through continual learning: an international multicentre study
